title: Chapter 1 — Eyes in the Willow Trees
content:
Parsons Manor stood like a stone sentinel amid the weeping willows, shrouded in perpetual coastal fog. When I inherited the gothic estate from my eccentric grandmother, I sought quiet refuge to write my novels—a solitary haven away from the suffocating glare of the city.

But solitude is an illusion when someone decides you belong to them.

It began with small things: a single black calla lily placed on the grand piano while I slept; my antique music box playing in the dead of midnight; the distinct scent of spiced whiskey and rainwater lingering in my study after the French doors were locked tight.

Tonight, standing on the balcony as thunder shook the Victorian eaves, I saw him.

A tall silhouette stood at the edge of the iron gates, perfectly still in the torrential rain. His dark coat whipped in the gale, but his obsidian eyes were fixed straight on mine—unblinking, possessive, and terrifyingly patient.

A whisper of wind carried the chill into my bones. He wasn’t a ghost trying to haunt my house.

He was a predator, and I had just stepped into his cage.

title: Scene 2 — Challenging the Elders and the Oath
content:
=== SCENE 2 — CHALLENGING THE ELDERS AND THE OATH ===

Setting: the Secluded Gothic Estate of Parsons Manor. The atmosphere is charged with tension.

Adeline: "We have walked under this cloud long enough. If we do not speak now, the truth will be buried beneath the soil of our ancestors!"

Zade Meadows: "Do you dare defy the council? Tradition was carved into stone long before your father learned to walk."

Adeline: "Tradition that suffocates its own children is not wisdom—it is fear wearing a crown. Today, we choose life."

The onlookers murmur. The drumbeats slow, then erupt in a rhythmic cadence that reverberates across the hills.

Zade Meadows: "Then let heaven be the judge between your conviction and our law."

With a decisive movement, Adeline turns toward the gathered assembly. The stage dims to an amber glow as destiny shifts into motion.
